speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head V of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our economic agencies have risen up to the occasion during this pandemic crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides the daunting healthcare challenges, we were also faced with multiple stresses on the economic front and also to ensure that supplies continue to flow into Singapore, especially essential items and necessities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For a small country with limited local resources, it is no small feat that we can continue to secure the adequate supplies needed, especially during the intense months when borders were closed and many countries restricted exports.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Armed with strong fiscal support and moratorium measures, the economic agencies went into overdrive mode to swiftly get these measures out to the businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It was timely enough to save many businesses and jobs and, importantly, prevent economic scarring.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I remember sending many emails to them, appeals and requests for assistance from our residents who were deeply impacted by the crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The ESG officers were always sympathetic and helpful to each of these requests and would duly close the loop with the residents and businesses with support, help and advice.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: During the most turbulent period of the crisis, I know that the ESG and MTI teams have gone out of the way to tap on their global networks to secure food items and other essential supplies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are real operations and I can imagine the responsibilities and pressure on the shoulders of the MTI and ESG officers during that period of time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This pandemic underscores the importance of resilience and diversification for our sources of essential supplies and the need for a robust stockpile policy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: COVID-19 also reminded us that we will still need to maintain a small but substantial part of manufacturing capabilities locally, which can be quickly scaled up in times of need.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These may well be low value-add production during peacetime but can suddenly become important critical resources in an unexpected crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, all these resilience-related contingent provisions would add further costs to Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It will also have structural implications to the overall economy and the cost of doing businesses here.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I hope that MTI can monitor this closely and look at how we can holistically optimise the overall costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is against a backdrop of falling global foreign direct investment (FDI) flows.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Other exciting and value-creating investments brought in last year include the Hyundai Motor Group Innovation Center, Siemens' Advance Manufacturing Transformation Center, Tata's Digital Acceleration Centre, and others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: EBD was able to sell Singapore as an open, trusted and connected hub that comes with a skilled talent pool, well-endowed capital, and a vibrant and innovative enterprise eco-system.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Together with our vibrant local enterprises and Singapore being a premiere financial centre, these new investments all add up to strengthening our position as a global-Asia node.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must build non-substitutable or sticky connectivity so as to maintain our competitive edge as a critical node.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, beside best-in-class physical connectivity, we also need to develop and enhance other centres-of-excellence such as digital connectivity, trade connectivity—even regulatory connectivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister for an update as to how we are enhancing Singapore's connectivity to the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In almost every Budget, there will be focuses and sizeable allocations targeted at helping businesses to transform, to build capabilities and to innovate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In more recent Budgets, we have also seen increased support in areas such as digitalisation and in developing sustainability as a competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to grow our local large enterprises (LLEs) into industry champions and also help promising medium-size companies grow to become LLEs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Catalysing a wide range of capital to help businesses transform and to scale is also one of the key enablers laid out in Budget 2021.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask for an update from the Minister as to how are we growing our local champions and how are we revving up the pace of transformation to achieve size and scale?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Also, has COVID-19 set us back on our internationalisation momentum?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given the various structural shifts as described in the Budget Statement, how will Singapore operate in the new global and regional landscape and stay competitive and relevant?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: One particular structural shift is in the reconfigured global supply chain.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, COVID-19 has accelerated the bifurcation of global trade and exposed the vulnerabilities in inter-connected supply chains.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As countries and companies rebuild business networks, relocate value chains and continue to de-couple, Singapore must work to stay relevant and position itself for the shifting economic landscape.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How has Singapore performed as an investment destination in the midst of the pandemic and what strategies is the Government pursuing to distinguish ourselves as a business hub?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore must redefine our competitive edge by pivoting towards innovation as a driver of growth and a vibrant digital economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask: what progress have we made to nurture a strong start-up eco-system and how does Singapore compare to other start-up eco-systems in Asia and across the world?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore is recognised globally for its leadership in the field of intellectual property protection and scientific research.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, are we attracting our fair share of deep-tech start-ups in search of robust IP protection?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To support the development of the digital economy, it is critical to offer corporations access to top-tech talent.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How is Singapore doing in our efforts to develop tech talent from our Institutes of Higher Learning as well as programmes, such as TechSkills Accelerator?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How successful has the Tech.Pass been in attracting established tech entrepreneurs, leaders or technical experts from around the world to come to Singapore, where they can nurture disruptive innovation?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic has also shown the world once again what we are capable of as a people and as a nation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In a fragmented world where trust is in short supply, this is the time that Singapore is well-positioned to capitalise on the premium for quality, resilience and neutrality, all of which play to Singapore’s strengths.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is an opportune time for Singapore to capitalise on our brand.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, whilst it is understandable that existing broad-based fiscal support cannot be sustained indefinitely, we should be cognisant that companies need time to recover.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Any premature withdrawal of support may undo the good work already invested to keep them afloat during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Companies should seize this additional funding to embark on transformation to reinvent and rejuvenate their business model.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In addition to Temasek, the Government should also consider the participation of other established private equity firms for more parties to contribute to the development of these local corporates.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Besides funding, we should support large local firms to access R&D in their pivot to new growth areas as well as higher value-added services and offerings.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They can also benefit from support in forging new partnerships locally as well as internationally.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can the Government spur partnerships with local corporations and the development of an integrated value chain that includes sub-contractors and service providers in Singapore, as well as opportunities to venture overseas together?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, the most vexing story of the COVID-19 pandemic has been that economies have to deal with damaging cyclical forces from the virus and accelerated structural changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Ironically, while the blueprint to manage the virus-related fall-out is perhaps seemingly clearer, that of the large structural forces are less understood.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has also questioned Singapore’s trade hub status.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 precipitated protectionism as countries critically re-examine the resiliency of their supply chains.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many vulnerabilities from long supply chains were unraveled.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Companies would now need to rebalance their supply chains to manage their risks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As a node for global supply chains, Singapore will now need to re-examine how it can stay competitive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is an added layer of complexity from the US-China tensions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Decisions on how and where to source for products and services are now mired in a web of trade tensions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Air travel and, consequently, aviation and hospitality sectors will change fundamentally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The ease of online collaboration would significantly alter our MICE activities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This has disrupted the eco-system of commercial activities that we had built up over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our hub strategy would need to adapt to the new trade climate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What are the global re-opening opportunities that we must seize now?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Larger companies with more resources are better prepared to deal with such changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Things are much less rosy for the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The changes will unduly affect them as they have less cash to manage disruptions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: SMEs must now cope with loan moratoriums and COVID-19-related measures coming to an end.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There will be SMEs that have yet to see a material rebound in fortunes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Amongst these SMEs could be good young start-ups.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Losing such innovative SMEs could mean setting back our entrepreneurship scene.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is value for us to pursue more of such programmes with our companies to help them drive better revenue growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, Singapore's economic transformation since independence has relied on integration into the global economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: That reliance came at a time when trade barriers that were set up during the Great Depression in the 1930s – a period of prolonged slump – were being dismantled.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, Singapore’s economic growth from the 1960s onwards rode on growing world trade.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Now, COVID-19, which has adversely affected both the advanced and emerging economies, can tend to cause countries to adopt inward-looking protectionist policies.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The question: how do we navigate a world of potentially more fractured globalisation?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: MTI, no doubt, must have devoted much time and energy to think about how the Singapore economy can still take advantage of economic openness to generate good jobs for our residents.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the challenges we face, this is the way to achieve the required productivity growth to support an economy that creates good jobs with good pay.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There are three, to my mind, potential sources of comparative advantage in the current circumstances.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: First, this comparative advantage could come through a so-called “home market” effect.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The demand for Singapore’s goods comes from both domestic sources as well as external sources.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A feature of the COVID-19 shock is that, broadly speaking, it affects two sectors unevenly – an affected sector, which includes aviation, aerospace and tourism, and a non-contact-intensive sector.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is a decline in demand for goods produced by the affected sector.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: How do we boost domestic demand for goods produced by the non-contact-intensive sector?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A key factor here is the degree of substitution between the goods produced by the affected sector and the goods produced by the non-contact-intensive sector.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Because of COVID-19, Singapore residents are unable to travel overseas for holidays.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In normal times, our local businesses would find it difficult to capture a large portion of the spending of Singapore residents because they would prefer to travel overseas for their holidays.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Now that it is difficult to travel overseas.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is, therefore, a natural advantage presented to our local entrepreneurs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This potentially means a larger domestic demand for the goods and services of our local businesses.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: If the trade association and chambers representing these local businesses can facilitate the organisation and marketing to reach these residents, we can lower the average cost of supplying the goods from the non-contact-intensive sector.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: These businesses can then charge a lower price as the whole industry enjoys economies of scale.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Even when COVID-19 is over, the experience of offering products to suit local customers’ tastes could well enable our innovators running these local firms to reach foreign customers as well.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Although there are fewer tourists walking down the streets to purchase from local firms, digitalisation might enable them to find an online platform to reach overseas customers who would have taken their holidays in Singapore in the absence of the pandemic.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: An example is to create a virtual experience for these foreign customers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Local firms can also build upon the digital platform to establish a business presence as part of the global value chain to supply intermediate products to foreign customers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Innovative firms engaged in R&D in clean technology will find it more profitable to undertake risky investments if it can find a sufficiently large market for its products.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore makes a commitment to adopt a whole-of-society approach to create an environmentally sustainable place to live, work and play in, this creates a larger demand for capital goods that embody this clean technology.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Having tested their products in the local Singapore market, these innovative firms can then potentially export such capital goods to the rest of the world.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In sum, there are still potential opportunities, despite the circumstances, to ride on global opportunities to grow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore provides amongst other things tax incentives for MNCs to set up regional headquarters and other investments because they contribute towards our economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But the pandemic has given us a sobering reminder that SMEs play on an unequal footing because of their smaller balance sheets and brand value.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: MNC investment is often attracted by incentive packages that include tax incentives and other forms of incentivisation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These are tied to economic targets like total business spending, fixed asset investment and headcount.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But, however, SMEs really grown into regional and global players helped by these schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In other countries in the region, MNCs are sometimes required to have a certain percentage of local equity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am not advocating that at this point as it may make us too uncompetitive to attract MNCs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, can I take my four cuts together?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With the growing importance of and the economic shift to Asia, Singapore is well positioned to be a more resilient and advanced manufacturing base in Asia for the world.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Many leading global companies have located their operations in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The Assessment Matrix has helped companies start, scale and sustain their Industry 4.0 transformation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How is Singapore continuing to promote Industry 4.0 adoption?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Against the backdrop of the current COVID-10 pandemic, how will Singapore continue to be an attractive manufacturing base and move up the value chain for these companies?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And how will Singapore continue to instill confidence for companies to build on their investments in production, headquarters, R&D and supply chain manufacturing functions in Singapore and to make Singapore the Asian node for their operations in the region?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What is the future of our manufacturing sector?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And how can Singapore ensure that our supply chain remains resilient in a post COVID-19 world?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The world is becoming more complex and there is greater inter-relationship across sectors and adjacent opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: We are seeing the growing importance of Asia as an engine for growth.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Digitalisation is accelerating and the growth of the digital economy has gained greater momentum with the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The disruptions have also highlighted the importance of resilience in our supply chain.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With climate change and the drive for sustainability, there is increased emphasis on sustainable products and services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With these trends, what are the growth and/or emerging sectors for Singapore?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How can we enable active participation of our local businesses in these sectors?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, accessing new markets can be challenging for any company, large or small.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With a small domestic market, increasing digitalisation and competition, Singapore companies cannot ignore the need to look beyond Singapore to grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Can Minister share how more local businesses can be supported to internationalise, grow and build capabilities to compete globally?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Apart from capital and funding support, these companies need to develop their talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And beyond talent, what support is available for our Singapore companies to access systems and platforms, know-how and networks to enter new markets.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Similar to how Alibaba’s Tmall has enabled global startups access the China e-commerce market.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How can Trade Associations and Chambers of Commerce or other bodies be encouraged to play a stronger role in helping businesses overcome internationalisation challenges?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How can we encourage more SMEs to transform and adopt digital solutions to improve productivity in the face of manpower and cashflow challenges?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What support will the Government provide to SMEs intending to digitalise?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With the many different schemes to support businesses, understandably, there is also a myriad of support schemes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: So, how can Government support schemes be streamlined and made more accessible for businesses, especially our SMEs?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: A key part of enterprise development is access to talent.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: How is Singapore developing our pipeline of local tech talent?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What resources are being directed towards improving the training and upskilling of local SME workers for technology-related roles and innovation?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, we are fortunate that Singapore has adequate financial resources and is willing to think ahead by investing in RIE or Research, Innovation and Enterprise to future-proof our society and economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The next RIE budget for 2021 to 2025 calls for another $25 billion of spending.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What does that say about our progress in building up our domestic research talent pool over the last two decades?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In our opinion, it is premature to increase research expenditure significantly when we still lack a sizeable domestic pool of research talent.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, besides looking at the research component of the RIE budget, the Government should also conduct a review of the allocation of resources used to promote innovation and enterprise.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From my humble experience as a venture capitalist, new ventures cannot be effectively promoted by the Government using co-funding.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is because the limited number of public servants would not be able to assess the potential of thousands of venture ideas emerging at any one time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is better to let the private sector do the job.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this way the capital can be channeled into proper use to help us to become a regional venture capital hub for both Singaporean and foreign ventures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should confine and expand its role as a facilitator by helping local ventures through its procurement policies, which my colleague Hazel Poa has brought up in her speech, through buying local products to boost their credibility and through providing facilities for testing and commercialisation for many more companies apart from the selective few presently.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence we urge the Government to relook at the allocation of resources to Research, Innovation and Enterprise in order to achieve better outcomes for Singaporeans and for our the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Chairman, I wish to declare that I work at a research-oriented Institution of Higher Learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has few firms for which intangible assets make up the majority of the balance sheet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even one of the top Singapore-based Internet and E-commerce firms, SEA Limited, reports that only about 1% of its assets are intangible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is solid evidence that R&D investments can improve and be a boost to productivity via catalytic effects on innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The need to boost productivity is especially poignant in light of Singapore's poor productivity performance and in effect that has been collaborated study after study.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It can also pay for itself since heightened productivity would itself grow out our GDP pie.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Increases in national expenditure appropriately directed for R&D is, therefore, an evidently attractive avenue for not just boosting productivity and, therefore, growth but also helping companies and our people stay at the forefront of advances in the digital economy and other artificial intelligence revolution, green technologies, modern manufacturing and biotech innovations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Civil servants responsible for disbursing grant support for firms confidentially share that they often face difficulty in identifying and allocating grant financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They add that local businesses remain reluctant to fully embrace R&D, even where financial support is available.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is critical that we convince as many local firms as possible, especially those in the SME sector, that their continued success hinges on cultivating and embedding an innovative mindset.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Just as pertinent, we have to be sensitive to the transition process and channel R&D funds away from certain industries that our economy has traditionally relied on such as petrochemicals, wholesale trading or back-office finance that we deem to be inconsistent with our 21st century economic model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Instead, we can re-direct R&D grants and subsidies toward the sunrise industries that the Government has already identified.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The vast majority of our government grants via A*STAR or IMDA, even when not explicitly earmarked for technology start-ups, are still heavily directed towards supporting business digitalisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While important, innovation may occur in unexpected ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, we can look at the continued refinement of modern Singapore cuisine, developing new techniques for sustainable landscaping and energy efficient building design, pioneering new elderly care methodologies, or identifying new tools to support advanced manufacturing, as Minister Heng has already emphasised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More generally, candidate projects with the highest probability of success are seldom best identified via tightly defined conditions, which speaks to the need for us to be more accommodating in our assessment methods and more liberal in our qualification criteria for Government R&D grants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This amount, to be funded from public and private sources, will ostensibly be directed toward a broad range of innovative activity across the economy and especially in existing SMEs with innovative activity.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, this news brings hope – hope of a Singaporean worker who looks forward to seizing opportunities for such high value-added jobs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, union leaders are curious to know how our locals can seize such job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Such good jobs, we hope, will be able to lure the younger generation of ITE and Polytechnic graduates into the workforce early or even narrow the unemployment of our locals over the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: From the good news requires actions to get ready the workforce for type of skills and knowledge required.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Information and knowledge actions will certainly give us more lead way to identify workers and training institutions to help prepare our workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: On behalf of fellow leaders from NTUC, we look forward to working closely with MTI and EDB to prepare our Singaporean workers to seize such high value-added jobs when the companies come on board.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We want every worker to aspire for such jobs, as every worker should aspire to for better job, better work prospects, for a better life for themselves and their families.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I would like to take both cuts together.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Mr Chairman, let me start by recollecting a meeting I had organised for a IBM Senior Vice President to call on the then Singapore EDB MD, Mr Lim Swee Say.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: During the meeting, Mr Lim asked a question which stuck in my head for good, and it goes something like this: “How can Singapore stay relevant to IBM’s growth ambitions and global strategies?” After the meeting, the IBM SVP shared with me that no country has ever framed a question like that before!

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: IBM was surely impressed, to say the least.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: That year, IBM established its first disk drive manufacturing facility in ASEAN, right here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: And this track record persists even in COVID-19 year, as hon Member Liang Eng Hwa has shared earlier.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: The Singapore EDB is an amazing marketing machinery in selling the advantages of Singapore and “bidding” for jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Attracting the MNCs to our shores amidst competitive landscape is a feat in itself but what makes Singapore stand out is that Singapore delivers on our promise; a) with the Singaporean workers who are skilled, hardworking and principled; b) with Singapore companies that have the capabilities to be plugged into the MNC’s global eco-system; c) with our efficient government systems and non-corrupt business practices; and d) with Singapore being the open and global city that is attractive to the best of global expertise and diversity of brain power.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: This has been what makes Singapore, a small economy, break out from the rest.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: In recent times, there have been rumblings of “foreigners taking our jobs”.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: For MTI and EDB, in their engagement with the MNCs to lean-in on the value of the Singapore talent as the foundation of their business success.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: According to a McKinsey Study, post-COVID-19, we will see “remote work” on the rise.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: In other words, companies do not need to bring the foreign talents on-shore as they can distribute the work off-shore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Can the Minister share the Government’s strategy to maintain or even enhance our hub status?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: For me, I believe that a new social compact in the workplace is one of the critical factors.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: For my fellow Singaporean PMETS, we need to acknowledge that foreign talents do complement Singapore talents.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Asking “who has moved my cheese?” will not help.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Having the skills to do the job is but minimum expectation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: According to a February 2021 Singapore Human Resource Institute study, employers increasingly look for critical attributes such as a growth mindset, a risk-taking attitude and a drive to excel.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Our Singapore workforce and us as parents to the next generation workforce, must “wake up” from our unrealistic expectations, seize the day and bounce back with our classic Singaporean “Can Do” attitude.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I am sure that the selected LLEs will benefit not only from the additional capital injected by this fund but will also benefit from Temasek’s leadership development, mentoring, and access to networks and tools, which will further enable the LLEs to accelerate their becoming potential local champions.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I have a few questions and one idea for the Minister with regards this purposeful proposition.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: One, that criteria must the LLE fulfil for the company to be eligible to be a “target” investment for this Fund?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Two, assuming that there will be an over-whelming response from the LLEs, how will Temasek and MTI decide which LLEs to fund?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: For example, sector specific, green future and so on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Three, will this "Local Enterprises Funding Platform" initiative be extended to support SMEs as well?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: In Singapore, we have many SMEs which may be "stuck" due to lack of capital, lack of access to tools and networks especially for going beyond Singapore, and lack of leadership and expert capabilities needed to breakout and stand out.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: If we can lift our SMEs, it will be a lift for the Singapore workforce.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: And, finally, I would like to offer an idea – perhaps, there is an opportunity for the LLEs to play "Queen Bee", to bring along the SMEs in their value-chain, and be funded as a portfolio of companies in a value-chain, under this initiative.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: This could empower the players to hunt in a pack, and thereby strengthening overall competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: SMEs face many challenges in attracting and retaining local talent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There is sometimes a bias against working for SMEs in favour of MNCs, GLCs or the Civil Service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many SMEs try their best to attract local talent, for example, by offering competitive salaries, but with mixed results.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to help our SMEs attract more local talent if we are to nurture globally competitive, homegrown firms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I propose three ways to help them achieve this.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, in both the classroom and at home, teachers and parents could encourage our young people to broaden their career aspirations and widen their definition of success.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Not every child needs to aspire to be a doctor, lawyer, banker or government scholar.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many SMEs provide incredible opportunities to learn different skills and take on multiple roles.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, there needs to be a rebranding of SMEs as employers of choice.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We could do more to profile SMEs both in the media, and also as business case studies within classrooms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They could be provided easier access to certified executive coaches who can provide one-to-one guidance on improving their management approaches.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I believe all these could help our local SMEs become more attractive workplaces for Singaporeans to work and enlarge the SMEs' talent pool.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, SMEs have the potential to significantly boost economic growth.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is known that the productivity gap between large companies and SMEs can vary in several multitudes depending on the industry.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, helping to raise the productivity of SMEs can be a worthwhile endeavour given the potential upside and the ability to drive economic growth within the country.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: SMEs are better positioned to integrate proven practices and technologies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And they also have more agility and are at less risk in testing and adopting new technologies, especially technologies and processes of large companies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At the same time, SMEs can be more innovative.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As SMEs are usually unencumbered by large systems and outdated strategies, they are often able to rethink established practices and cut through traditional industry boundaries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, the lack of resources and access to talent continues to pose implementation challenges for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Limited awareness of digital solutions, limited access to digital talent, and limited capital to invest in digital technologies can hinder the uptake of these technologies by SMEs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Governments have started expanding their productivity programmes toward digital adoption and started dedicated programs to help SMEs deploy more productive digital processes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: One good example we could learn from is the Mittelstand 4.0 centres of excellence in Germany.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As shared in a McKinsey report, in Finland, the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment and several technology industries have launched an accelerator dedicated to helping firms deploy digital solutions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The accelerator offers six-month programmes for companies that have already piloted AI application on products and services.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: About 15 Finnish companies provide funding and technical support to the accelerator.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Then, these organisations would work with service providers, start-ups, academia in short sprints to help deploy the AI applications or the deliverables.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The first batch of companies from accelerator, for example, would work together to then deploy speech recognition technologies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Some companies progress by fusing physical and cyber realms.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: One such local company come to my mind.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Leon, the founder of a local watch company, BOLDR, has a global franchise.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They are amongst the first to build a mechanical watch with digital functions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: With two full-time employees, Yong Hong and Jaspo, they design, build and supply watches using Sellita and ETA movements.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Watch enthusiasts would know that these are very high quality movements.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As the name of the company represents – BOLDR – we too can help SMEs tackle challenges and develop their capability to expand further.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To secure Singapore's future we must be able to build an innovative eco-system that has the ability to grow and compete globally.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: PACT should be the first port of call grant for all enterprises to encourage companies to collaborate and achieve greater economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Government funding will also be maximised as it impacts two or more businesses and their employees.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Due to our small domestic economy base, it is crucial that we foster a collaborative and partnership mindset amongst companies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such joint venture projects and collaborations can be preludes to deeper partnerships such as actual mergers and acquisitions as company founders, directors and employees develop trust and relationships with each other.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is crucial in our efforts to scale up SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This complements the Deputy Prime Minister's announcement of a joint Government investment with Temasek Holdings to invest in our LLEs as it provides a pipeline of SMEs that could grow to become LLEs or be combined with LLEs via mergers and acquisitions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, in the past year, industry players in the tourism sector have made many changes to survive in this challenging climate.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the hard truth remains that we are a small market and we need to be realistic about the current lower appetite for international leisure travel.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nonetheless, we should use the crisis as an opportunity to drive innovation and improve productivity and boost Singapore's profile as a safe, secure, efficient and exciting destination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we continue to enhance infrastructural and product development in the industry to ensure that Singaporeans want to holiday at home and that we can compete in international markets?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can also plan to run more safe and secure major events designed to assist in the global recovery from COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can we invest efficiently in the sector to keep it afloat while keeping losses minimal?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, may I take cuts (u) and (v) together?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: As the economic recovery will take longer, some business segments will experience a flatter K-shape recovery.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: What are other non-financial support will be provided to help boost SME services to help them ride out this pandemic situation?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: SMEs are doing what they can to do more business, so in place of subsidies, will the Government be planning to bring forward contracts to support the demand for SME services?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Given this, what other plans does the Government have in place for the tourism sector beyond the Resilience Package?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Many of our residents will not have the opportunity to travel and have been keen to explore more of Singapore, as observed from the experience of the last December holidays.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Will the Minister consider accelerating domestic tourism for our citizens to further explore Singapore's nature and arts and culture scene to help our local businesses?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: We have been striving to help strengthen our SME businesses.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: It is a known fact that they are often faced by challenges, such as the lack of business size and scale, and as a result, face challenges in adopting technology solutions that could generally be costly on a standalone basis, but could perhaps be a lot more affordable if adopted across a segment of the industry.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: SME entrepreneurs want to focus on their business and many are not tech savvy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: They want to see more help – from an economic standpoint of technology service as a platform.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: So, for one, they will not see the incurrence of capital cost, since grants generally do not cover 100% of the initiative; and secondly, they want to minimise risk since they do not know if the benefits of the technology solution will pay off.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Given situations like this, what will the Government do more of and differently beyond providing grants to better encourage and guide our enterprises to adopt technology and digital solutions to improve productivity?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: From a trade associations and chambers of commerce (TACs) standpoint, they also have a role to play, given their influence through their long-standing relationships with their members.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh
text: Can the Minister explain what the progress has been in this space so far, and if TACs can play a part to help aggregate the demand for such information and communications technology (ICT) needs to further complement the efforts of the Government to deliver more economical solutions for the respective segments in their industries?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Chairman, let me first thank all the Members for their questions and many useful suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I would also like to thank the many Members who have spoken kind words on the work that MTI has done over the last one year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Chairman, over the past week, much has been discussed about how we should or should not use our reserves, and how we can and we should – and we want to – do many more things for various groups in our society.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, we must not lose sight that first and foremost, we need to earn our keep – for this and future generations – under the shadow of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are still trying to get out of the most serious recession since Independence.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are not returning to a pre-COVID-19 world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Even if our gross domestic product (GDP) returns to a pre-COVID-19 level, quantitatively, we will have a qualitatively different economy then.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The share of sectors and industries will be different.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The types of products and services that we produce and trade with the world will be different.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The skillsets of our people required to make a living will be different.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must start now to build this new economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The rollout of vaccines across the world is uneven and this will complicate countries' recovery from the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: All countries have spent an extraordinary amount of fiscal resources to stabilise their economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many, if not all of them, will contest for fiscal revenue, possibly leading to tax policies that will distort investment, production and trade.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The rules-based global trading order, underpinned by the proper functioning of the World Trade Organization (WTO), is straining.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Global supply chains are being re-ordered and re-configured, not always for economic reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Desmond Choo asked how we can remain competitive and relevant amidst these disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to turn these challenges into opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must be a safe harbour for capital, talent and ideas in an uncertain world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must be connected, trusted and resilient, as a node, both physically and virtually, in order to serve different markets in a bifurcating and fragmenting world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to embrace technology, especially digital technology – to be the disruptor and not be the disrupted.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We need to master digitalisation to transcend the constraints of our size and geographical location, where mastery of data can lead to increasing returns to scale.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And we need to leverage on our small size to pivot faster and to respond more nimbly than our competitors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Over the last six months, MTI has visited our companies every week to see how we can work with them to overcome the immediate challenges but more importantly, to seize the opportunities going forward.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These plans have been widely reported in the media and I will not repeat all of them today.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Instead, I will draw together three broad strategies that we must execute well, consistently and coherently.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These are votes of confidence and faith in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We should be proud of how we have responded, but we must press on.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The ease of digital connection, collaboration, supervision and even execution will redefine the role of hubs for businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Lower value-added activities will increasingly be off-shored to remote working sites, as they are no longer constrained by geographical boundaries.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Work from home means work from anywhere around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Competition will never be local but always global.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: However, the world will still need high quality business hubs for high value-add transactions and trusted collaborations that must be executed via physical interactions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For Singapore to be in this global class of the few high-quality, high-trust business hubs, we will need to create an environment where we distinguish ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And this is how we are going to do it.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, with clear, transparent, consistent and coherent legal and policy frameworks to allow businesses to mobilise capital, aggregate talent and protect intellectual property.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, with progressive rules to enable new business models to thrive.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Third, with superior networks that give us denser and more secured connections with the world, allowing global businesses to operate out from Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Next, with a mix of global and local talent to serve diverse markets across the entire globe.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And finally, to entrench critical parts of the R&D value chains, so that businesses will include us in their innovation networks, even in the depth of any crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These are the reasons why we are investing heavily in the development of our local talent, the attraction of global talent to complement and reinforce our local talent pool.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is also why we are aggressively strengthening our physical trade and digital connectivity including expanding our network of Free Trade Agreements and the new generation of digital agreements and partnerships.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is also why we have spent and will continue to spend on our R&D – from basic research to translational research for commercialisation, and this also why – as we have heard from MinLaw – we will continue to strengthen our IP regime, from valuation to arbitration and assessment so that we provide a complete eco-system for businesses wanting to put their IP in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must get all these enablers right, to strengthen our position as a global business hub.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: With all these enablers in place, we are confident that our reputation as a trusted and efficient place to do business will distinguish us from the competition.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But, we are not complacent and we must never be complacent.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are always very aware of the stiff competition that we are up against.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about growth sectors, and how we can seize opportunities in the re-organisation of the global supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are looking out for emerging sectors such as agri-tech, urban mobility and sustainable urban solutions, as Prof Hoon Hian Tech has mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Minister of State Alvin Tan will elaborate on how we will help local businesses venture into the agri-tech sector.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How much we produce and how much global market share we command now may not be the most important question over the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Moving further upstream, do we have the talent and talent networks to continuously innovate, to improve our processes and quality control, so that global companies will want to site their operations in Singapore and create better jobs for our people?

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These questions apply to high-tech industries like semiconductors, biomedical, and info-communications; as much as they apply to precision engineering and even to the manufacturing of the humble surgical masks.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Recently, I visited various enterprises and research institutes to better understand the new world of manufacturing to see how they incorporate Industry 4.0 technologies from data analytics to additive manufacturing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: A product that used to require many parts to assemble, can now be produced as one simple part, with additive manufacturing enabling, with much less wastage and much greater precision.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: A product that used to take years to evolve can now be designed and redesigned in days.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: A production system that used to be put together only after the product design has been finalised, is now being put together while the product design is being conceptualised.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The speed of evolution of products and production system is amazing.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And we need to understand all these changes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The ability to set standards for adoption in a fast-paced market has become critical to a product's success.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The "good enough" and fastest, will beat the better but slower.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There is much that we need to learn and change our mindset in this new, competitive environment.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Doing what others do at a cheaper price, is "Red Ocean Strategy".

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In other words these are shark-infested waters, best avoided.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Producing things that others cannot, is "Blue Ocean Strategy".

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Similarly, we can no longer be a place of arbitrage.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In a globalised world, we will be easily disintermediated and displaced by cheaper competitors or digital platforms, unless we can add something unique and of value to others.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must become the exchange that adds value.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The value-add can be the provision of complementary services or adjacent services, from financing, to legal to business syndication.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: It can also be in terms of verification and traceability in a world that is increasingly conscious about sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Prof Hoon Hian Teck spoke about enhancing connectivity and taking advantage of our economic openness.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Indeed, our superior connectivity will be a value-add factor in a world seeking greater resilience and diversity in their supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have here a deep and wide collection of global and local companies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This allows the companies located here to compete as an eco-system.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And I want to emphasise this: we compete as an eco-system.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In turn, our ecosystem attracts more companies to situate themselves here to take advantage of this superior network and the dense eco-system.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is now a virtuous cycle that was hard-fought and hard-won.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The IMF already ranks us a one of the world's most competitive economy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But, this is a journey without end and we must continue to invest in their capabilities and skills.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is why, I agree with Ms Janet Ang about about creating a new compact among businesses, employees and the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will spare no effort to help our enterprises and workers acquire new capabilities to compete in a more globalised world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We cannot shield ourselves from global competition, but we can and must equip ourselves to compete globally.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Businesses can play a role in this, together with Government and the unions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must all play our part to develop the local talent and grow Singaporeans to take on leadership positions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Singaporeans must also be prepared to venture overseas to seize new growth opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These are the correct ways forward for a small economy like ours.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: To deepen our corporate capabilities requires an eco-system approach.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must leverage on our existing strengths in tradition industries such as aerospace and manufacturing, even as we invest in emerging technologies like digital services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We must continue to attract global companies and MNCs with cutting edge business concepts and technologies to be planted here while we nurture our SMEs to be future global champions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I always tell our SMEs, "Stop calling yourselves 'small, medium enterprises'.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Aspire to be Singapore MNCs Emerging SMEs." Mr Leon Perera asked about the grants given to MNCs versus SMEs and suggested to tie a conditional incentive for MNCs to work with local SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I am glad Mr Leon Perera shares our philosophy.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But looking merely at relative grant amounts versus returns and value-adds overly simplifies the situation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, the relationship between MNCs and local companies is often symbiotic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And we will do more where it makes sense to.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, our support for MNCs and SMEs serve to enhance their symbiotic relationship in various ways.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our support helps them to bring in new business lines and technology that will uplift our entire eco-system and create high value-added jobs here.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For SMEs, we provide support for more fundamental purposes: digitalising, entering into new markets and streamlining work processes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: As smaller businesses level up, they will also grow to become an integral part of the local supplier eco-system for MNCs and beyond.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ms Jessica Tan asked how we can enable the active participation of local businesses in emerging sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We have different schemes to help companies big and small – because their needs are different.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For large enterprises, our goal is to help them compete globally by providing access to superior trade networks, R&D and talent networks.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will help them become regional or global champions, by providing growth capital and support for the commercialisation of R&D.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Schemes like the Market Readiness Assistance grants help them to penetrate overseas markets.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second Minister Tan See Leng will share more on the support available for different enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For small and micro-enterprises, our goal is to provide them with shared and digital platforms to improve their productivity and efficiencies by accessing shared capabilities, from design to sales to management.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Minister of State Low Yen Ling and Minister of State Alvin Tan will share more.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are never shy to do away with old schemes that are no longer relevant, no longer needed, or are less relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We will constantly re-invest our finite resources into the schemes that do the best, the most, for our enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Chairman and Members of this House, let now me reiterate where I left off at the beginning.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are not returning to a pre-COVID-19 world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: How we make a living will change even faster in the days ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Let us and let us help our people, focus our minds on the new forms of competition ahead, for it will be tougher, it will be more global.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Let us not focus on the wrong issues or try to resist inevitable change, or try to protect what will be made irrelevant and displaced in time to come.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Ultimately, our ability to do many of the good things that we have said in this House rests on our ability to earn our keep and make a living in this more globalised, more competitive world and we must never forget that.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Let us face up to the competition, do the right things, help our enterprises and people acquire a competitive advantage to distinguish ourselves from the competition.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: COVID-19 is said to be the crisis of our generation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This can also be the opportunity of our generation to distinguish ourselves, to lay the foundation for the next generation, by winning new investments and creating better jobs for this generation and the next.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I have every confidence that if anyone in the world can do this, Singapore and Singaporeans must be amongst them, and we will emerge stronger together from this crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Chairman, I shall speak about two ways through which we will help our enterprises emerge stronger from the crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, by anchoring strong local enterprises; and, second, by helping our enterprises go global.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Shawn Huang asked how we intend to support businesses and nurture them into local champions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will do so by pressing on with industry transformation at both the sector level and, contemporaneously, at the eco-system level.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our overriding priority over the past one year has been to weather the COVID-19 storm.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We must keep our eyes focused on the future and press on with industry transformation to emerge stronger.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We had earlier embarked on transformation through our 23 Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) and we are refreshing them to make sure that they are still relevant in light of COVID-19, and that we are able to unlock new opportunities that have arisen globally over the last 12 months or so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa also asked how we will turn up the pace of transformation and we will do this by strengthening our industrial ecosystem and accelerating Industry 4.0 or the I4.0 adoption.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One example of this is the manufacturing industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is fundamentally changing with digitalisation, robotics and new technologies like additive manufacturing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The industry needs to transform to achieve our manufacturing 2030 vision and we are taking decisive steps to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Smart Industry Readiness Index or SIRI launched in 2017 helps manufacturing firms take specific, measurable steps towards transformation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are working with the World Economic Forum (WEF) to make SIRI a global benchmark to facilitate our SIRI assessed firms to be able to compete globally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The JTC-SBF Industry Transformation Initiative, which was launched last year, will further help local manufacturing companies in their I4.0 transformation, by providing access to resources like curated training workshops and capability building initiatives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also create new peaks of manufacturing excellence by bringing together related companies to collaborate, to experiment and to succeed together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Just as Jurong Island and the Seletar Aerospace Park catalyse our chemicals and aerospace industries respectively in the not-too-distant past, so too will the new Jurong Innovation District or JID be the catalyst for I4.0 ambitions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The JID will house the Advanced Remanufacturing and Technology Centre (ARTC) and factories of the future, and it will serve as the focal point to develop and testbed new technologies like 5G and autonomous vehicles to serve global markets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I4.0 is most commonly associated with the manufacturing sector but, actually, the spirit behind it – one of being forward-looking and making the most of technology, finding ways to do things more efficiently and smartly – must be a pervasive culture for all of us.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It has to apply aggressively across all industries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And I am happy today that many of our companies have imbibed this spirit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Besides sector-level transformation, as I have alluded to earlier on, we will also do more at the eco-system level to nurture all businesses, regardless of size and sector, to pursue the next bound of growth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In 2020, we enhanced co-funding schemes such as the Enterprise Development Grant (EDG) and Productivity Solutions Grant (PSG) to help companies transform their capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also continue strengthening enterprise leadership capabilities through schemes like the Enterprise Leadership for Transformation (ELT) and Scale-up SG programmes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Chairman, we will continue with this suite of support to strengthen enterprise capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister has spoken about the various scheme enhancements we will make to encourage more companies to come onboard.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One, a Team Singapore approach; two, access to financing; and, three, innovation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, a Team Singapore approach to capture opportunities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Edward Chia asked about how our companies can adopt a collaborative mindset such that the entire value chain is uplifted, and everyone benefits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Indeed, we must embrace this Team Singapore approach.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Because our competition is not with one another here, it is with the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, individually, even our largest companies are modest by international standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But, collectively, we can win as Team Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are doing much more to develop our winning game plan.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government is partnering the private sector on the AfAs; these are Alliances for Action.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They bring together a diverse range of industry and public sector stakeholders to quickly seize opportunities in sectors, such as tourism, logistics and others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, the AfA on Smart Commerce has brought together industry players to pioneer new operating models, to digitalise and to diversify revenue streams.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Another example is how various industry stakeholders collaborated to create opportunities in the pandemic for the Meetings, Incentives, Conventions and Exhibitions (MICE) sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Safe and Innovative Visitor Experience AfA developed a prototype for hosting exhibitions safely amidst last year's pandemic and tested it in November last year at the TravelRevive tradeshow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This has attracted close to 1,000 attendees, comprising 65 foreign visitors from 14 different countries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It showed that Singapore remained open for business – successfully and safely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A big part of our ecosystem strategy is strengthening the partnerships between large and small companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Hence, I agree with Ms Janet Ang that LLEs can play an important role in uplifting our SMEs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: ESG’s PACT programme encourages such mutually beneficial partnership programmes between companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: PACT has supported more than 280 partnerships and benefited more than 1,500 Singapore-based firms since 2010.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The National Innovation Challenges, launched in 2020, also helps to catalyse cross-company partnerships to address sector-wide challenges.
